messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 65-year-old widowed project manager of Oceania descent, has been struggling with intense distress following his child's near-fatal illness. John's experience during that critical period left him deeply scarred, particularly by the harrowing hospital stays and medical procedures his child had to endure. Since then, John finds himself intensely triggered whenever he encounters people involved in those events—doctors, nurses, even other parents with sick children at the hospital. These triggers often lead to an overwhelming sense of breathlessness, leaving him feeling short of breath as if something ominous is about to happen again. Each time a medical examination or procedure comes up, John experiences intense physical reactions, his heart racing and sweat breaking out on his forehead. He has come to believe that these events are reminders of the trauma he faced, and each trigger reawakens those painful memories. John's self-blame has been particularly pervasive; he harbors deep-seated guilt, believing that if only he had acted differently or more decisively, his child might have been spared such agony. This sense of failure to protect his child fuels his overwhelming negative emotions—fear, horror, anger, and shame—which in turn drive his maladaptive strategies for coping. John often tries hard not to think about the trauma, engaging in constant mental distractions by keeping himself busy with work and other activities. John's self-doubt compounds these feelings of inadequacy. He cannot trust that he will do the right thing when faced with similar situations again, which amplifies his fear and anxiety. This cycle has led him to avoid all medical cues—hospitals, ambulances, physical examinations—and whenever something takes longer than expected, John assumes something bad is happening. For instance, in his role as a project manager, delays or unexpected complications trigger these fears, making it difficult for him to remain focused and productive. His colleagues have noticed that he becomes increasingly agitated during stressful deadlines or when projects are delayed, often leading to conflicts at work. John's avoidance behaviors, such as staying away from hospitals and medical procedures, stem directly from his negative appraisals and self-doubt. He has come to believe that if he faces these cues again, the trauma will be reawakened with renewed intensity. This belief makes him more vigilant about avoiding any reminders of the event. Over time, John's symptoms have escalated, leading him to withdraw from social interactions and family gatherings. His wife, though supportive, finds it challenging to understand his growing isolation. The culmination of these issues finally prompted John to seek help. He is deeply afraid that he will never be able to fully escape the grip of this trauma but hopes that with support, he can learn to manage his reactions and regain a sense of control over his life. John’s journey towards healing begins with understanding and addressing the underlying cycle of triggers, negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and heightened threat perception. He is determined to break free from the self-reinforcing loop that has been consuming him for so long.
